Person.comment:
Ron Caspi received his PhD in Marine Microbiology in 1996 from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography in La Jolla, CA, under the guidance of Dr. Bradley Tebo and Dr. Margo Haygood. He completed his post-graduate education in 1999 with Dr. Donald Helinski at the Center for Molecular Genetics at UC San Diego.

After three years with Pangene Corporation, where he managed the automation and bioinformatics department, Ron joined SRI International in 2004, and has been the head curator of the MetaCyc database ever since.

Protein.comment:
Salmonella enterica degrades ethanolamine by a pathway dependent on adenosylcobalamin, a required cofactor of EC 4.3.1.7, ethanolamine ammonia-lyase (see ethanolamine utilization). The ethanolamine utilization (eut) operon includes all the genes that are necessary for the conversion of inactive cobalamins, such as vitamin B12, to adenosylcobalamin. One of these genes is eutT, which encodes an EC 2.5.1.154, corrinoid adenosyltransferase EutT.

Salmonella enterica possesses three adenosyltransferases that show no obvious amino acid sequence similarity. corrinoid adenosyltransferase CobA is the housekeeping enzyme, and participates in the de novo biosynthesis of adenosylcobalamin as well as the recycling of cobinamides. PduO is involved in (S)-propane-1,2-diol degradation, and is only induced in the presence of (S)-propane-1,2-diol. Similarly, EutT participates in ethanolamine utilization and is induced only in the presence of ethanolamine. Its main role is to convert inactive cobalamins to adenosylcobalamin specifically for the use of EC 4.3.1.7, ethanolamine ammonia-lyase.

The actual substrate for the enzymatic reaction is cob(I)alamin, in which the cobalt ion has a valency of +1. However, cob(I)alamin is very reactive, and, if left unprotected, is rapidly oxidized to cob(II)alamin. The midpoint redox potential of the Co2+/Co1+ couple is -610 mV, which is is too low for any known cellular reductant [Lexa76]. Remarkably, the enzyme is able to overcome this thermodynamic barrier. After binding cob(II)alamin an L-phenylalanine residue displaces the 5,6-dimethylbenzimidazole lower ligand [Mera09], generating a four-coordinate cob(II)alamin intermediate, the reduction potential of which is higher by >250 mV, bringing it within physiological range [Stich05, Stich05a, Park08b]. The cobalt is subsequently reduced to the +1 valence. The source of the electron used for the reduction of the enzyme-bound cob(II)alamin to cob(I)alamin in vivo has not been established. However, CobA was shown to interact in vitro with flavodoxin A (FldA), and reduced FldA was shown to efficiently drive the adenosylation of cob(II)alamin [Fonseca01, Buan05]. Furthermore, free reduced flavins and non-specific flavoproteins can also reduce cob(II)alamin bound in the active site of the enzyme, leading to the suggestion that bona fide cobalamin reductases may not be necessary [Mera10].

The eutT gene was cloned and expressed in Escherichia coli, and the recombinant protein was partially purified. Extracts of strains expressing the gene were assayed in the presence of hydroxocobalamin, ATP, and titanium(III) citrate (which reduces hydroxocobalamin to cob(I)alamin), and showed 50- to 100-fold more adenosyltransferase activity than the control strain [Sheppard04].

In a subsequent study the enzyme was overproduced and enriched to approximately 70% homogeneity. The enzyme, which was produced as insoluble inclusion bodies, was solubilized by detergent, and its basic kinetic parameters were determined. Unlike CobA, EutT does not adenosylate either cob(I)inamide or cyanocob(III)alamin. In addition, while PduO and CobA eliminate the tripolyphosphate group of ATP as triphosphate, EutT produces diphosphate and phosphate, and is not inhibited by triphosphate [Buan06].

A later study managed to purify the enzyme to homogeneity in the absence of detergents. The gene was cloned with an N-terminal hexahistidine tag and a maltose-binding protein (MBP) tag in tandem and expressed in Escherichia coli. The recombinant protein was purified under anaerobic conditions, and the tags were subsequently removed.The purified enzyme converted cob(II)alamin to adenosylcobalamin in the presence of free dihydroflavins and ATP. The enzyme contained zinc, which is likely bound to a HX11CCXXC motif. However, the highest activity was observed with Fe(II) ions, and it was suggested that iron, rather than zinc, acts in vivo [Moore14].

It is believed that following the completion of the reaction, the enzyme interacts with the target protein, EC 4.3.1.7, ethanolamine ammonia-lyase, to ensure proper delivery of the cofactor. The concentrations of adenosylcobalamin are too low for simple diffusion. While this has not been shown for this enzyme, a similar phenomenon was demonstrated for a PduO enzyme from Methylorubrum extorquens, which transfers adenosylcobalamin directly to methylmalonyl-CoA mutase [Padovani08]
